newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Senate softens harsh immigration reform.
newsitem.headline: French Senate softens harsh immigration reform.

text.p: The French senate softened and then early on Friday approved a harsh immigration reform bill sought by the government to crack down on foreigners living illegally in France.
The measure, which the National Assembly had beefed up before voting to approve it in December, now goes back to the assembly for final consideration.

During three days of often emotional debate, opposition Socialists and Communists accused the centre-right majority of xenophobia and pandering to supporters of Jean-Marie Le Pen and his far-right National Front party ahead of 1998 general elections.
At one point, former Socialist justice minister Robert Badinter said the measure would help spread the Front's "xenophobic ideology, leading to what I call the Lepenisation of our minds".

But hardline Gaullist Interior Minister Jean-Louis Debre said that to solve the problem, "we must shoulder our responsibilities. We do so not with words but with actions...We cannot take the easy way out".

Before approving the measure by a vote of 220 to 96, however, senators softened some of the most controversial parts of the bill, which had been toughened in December by majority deputies dissatisfied with the government's proposals.

The senators voted to allow illegal immigrants to stay if they had lived in France more than 15 years, and it cut back a provision authorising the state to fingerprint all non-European foreigners seeking a residence permit.
It also cut back to one year from two the length of time that spouses of French citizens had to be married before they could obtain a residence permit.

But it approved a provision letting the state restrict the freedom to put up a foreigner in one's private home. Opponents had argued the provision would bring back the days of the Vichy wartime occupation when neighbours were encouraged to spy on each other.
There are about five million foreign nationals in France including about a million illegal entrants, most of them from third world states.

The Senate debate took on special significance because it took place just days before Sunday's run-off municipal election in Vitrolles, where National Front candidate Catherine Megret has taken a commanding lead in the first round of voting.
Should Megret win, Vitrolles would become the fourth city hall in National Front hands after Marignane, Orange and Toulon.
